figureFiles.caption: One piece is one turn of the Tetris core loop. Only the two blue steps belong to the player; everything else is the game responding. The purple feedback (for a game started at level 0) makes success in the loop speed up the loop itself.

In Slay the Spire, each turn of combat sits inside a run, and each run sits inside the long meta loop. Notice that every outer loop changes the material the inner loop works with: a card reward changes your next hand, and a new card in the pool changes your next rewards.

The three rules of Life speak only about single cells and their eight neighbors, yet the glider rebuilds itself one cell down and one cell to the right every four generations. The movement is a property of the pattern, not of any rule.

lesson.hook: On 21 December 2023, a 13-year-old in Oklahoma named Willis Gibson did something no human player had managed in the 34 years since Nintendo released *Tetris* for its home console: he played until the game itself broke. At level 157 the screen froze, and the only opponent left was the code. Gibson had not found a secret ending, because there is none. He had repeated one short cycle of actions (watch a piece fall, slide it, turn it, drop it into place) thousands of times, faster and more accurately than anyone before him. That cycle has barely changed since Alexey Pajitnov wrote the first version in Moscow in 1984, on a computer that could display only text characters. A loop of a few actions has held players for four decades, and this chapter is about how such loops are built.
lesson.overview: Chapter 1 described a game as a system of rules (mechanics) that produces behavior in play (dynamics) and, through it, experience (aesthetics). This chapter zooms in on the mechanics the player touches directly. Section 2.1 names a game’s verbs and its core mechanic. Section 2.2 shows how actions form loops at three time scales, from a single turn to months of play. Section 2.3 turns to game feel: why the same rules can feel crisp or sluggish, and what research says about juice. Section 2.4 explains emergence, the way a few simple rules can combine into play nobody wrote down. Throughout, *Tetris* (1984), *Super Mario Bros.* (1985) and *Slay the Spire* (2019) supply the examples, and the chapter ends with the first real design step on your pocket card game: defining its core loop.
objectives: Identify the verbs and core mechanic of a game and classify mechanics as primary or secondary.
Diagram a game’s core, session and meta loops and explain how each outer loop changes the loop inside it.
Explain game feel using Swink’s definition and evaluate the evidence on juice.
Distinguish games of emergence from games of progression and trace an emergent pattern back to the rules that produce it.
Define the core loop of your own pocket card game.

sections.title: Verbs and core mechanics
reading: Chapter 1 split a game into mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics, and argued that designers work from the mechanics outward. This section looks at mechanics from the player’s seat. Whatever the rulebook or the code says, the player meets the rules as a short list of things they can do. Designers call these the game’s **verbs**. In *Tetris* you can move a piece left or right, rotate it and make it fall faster. In *Super Mario Bros.* you can walk, run and jump. In *Slay the Spire* you can play a card, end your turn, choose a path on the map and choose a reward. Each list is short. A good first test of any design, including your own, is whether its verbs fit on a sticky note.

Two definitions are worth carrying around. Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman define a **core mechanic** as “the essential play activity players perform again and again in a game” [1]. Miguel Sicart offers a more exact version: game mechanics are “methods invoked by agents for interacting with the game world” [2]. His wording does two jobs. It says mechanics belong to agents, so an enemy that patrols a ledge has mechanics too. And it sorts mechanics into tiers: **core mechanics** are the ones agents use repeatedly to reach the state the game rewards; **primary mechanics** are those a player can apply directly to beat a challenge; **secondary mechanics** make the goal easier without being necessary [2]. In *Super Mario Bros.*, jumping is primary. Throwing fireballs, possible only after you collect a Fire Flower, is secondary.

A verb on its own is cheap. What makes it a mechanic worth designing is what it acts on and what changes afterward. *Tetris* has three verbs, but they act on seven different pieces, the tetrominoes, in a well 10 cells wide and 20 tall, and every placement changes the board the next piece will fall into. Leave a hole and you have made a problem for your future self. Keep one column open and you are setting up a **tetris**, four lines cleared at once, the move the game rewards most. The decision is never just whether to rotate. It is what board you want three pieces from now. Ernest Adams and Joris Dormans make the same point about whole games: rules matter less one by one than as a system in which each action changes the state the next action works on [3].

Good verbs often do several jobs at once. Mario’s jump lifts him upward, but in World 1-1 the same button press also stomps a Goomba, bumps a question-mark block to release a coin or a mushroom, carries him over pipes and gaps and, at the end, onto the flagpole. One verb meets many objects, and each object answers it differently. Compare a game that gives the player a separate button for every task: more verbs, but fewer interesting combinations. When designers praise a game’s core mechanic, they usually mean this economy. A few verbs, each useful in many situations, mean that the skill a player builds with them keeps paying off.

To find a game’s verbs, start with the inputs and translate them into intentions. A controller has buttons; a player has goals. In *Tetris* the inputs are a direction pad and two rotation buttons, and the verbs are slide, rotate and drop. In *Slay the Spire* nearly every input is a mouse click, yet the verbs are richer: attack, block, weaken an enemy, draw, spend energy, skip a reward. Card games are built largely from verbs that move cards between zones: draw (deck to hand), play (hand to table), discard (hand to discard pile), trade, steal, reveal. Your pocket card game from Chapter 1 already has verbs, even if you have not named them yet. The challenge at the end of this chapter asks you to write them down.

keyTerms.def: An action the player can choose to take, such as jump, rotate or play a card.
The essential activity players perform again and again in a game.
In Sicart’s terms, a mechanic the player can apply directly to overcome a challenge.
In Sicart’s terms, a mechanic that makes reaching the goal easier but is not required.
Everything about the game at one moment, such as the board, the hand or the score, which each action changes.

example.title: Worked example: listing the verbs of World 1-1
steps: List the inputs. The NES controller offers a direction pad, an A button and a B button.
Translate inputs into verbs. Left and right walk; holding B while walking runs; A jumps, and holding it longer jumps higher; down enters certain pipes. After a Fire Flower, B also throws fireballs.
List what the jump acts on in 1-1: Goombas (stomp), question-mark blocks and bricks (bump from below), pipes and gaps (clear), and the flagpole (finish). No other verb touches so many objects.

Classify with Sicart’s tiers. Jumping is primary: you cannot finish the level without it. Fireballs are secondary: optional, and only available after a power-up. Running is subtler: it rarely beats a challenge alone, but it changes how far every jump carries.
Conclude that the core mechanic is the jump, shaped by running, because it is used constantly and almost every object in the level responds to it.
example.takeaway: A verb is worth more when more things in the game world respond to it.

misconception.myth: A game’s core mechanic is its theme, like space exploration or running a farm.
misconception.fact: The theme is what the game is about; the core mechanic is what the player repeatedly does. Two farming games can have entirely different core mechanics (one about planting on a timer, one about trading cards), and *Tetris* has a strong core mechanic with no theme at all.

practice.q: Using Sicart’s tiers, which of these is a secondary mechanic in Super Mario Bros.?
choices: Jumping
Throwing fireballs after collecting a Fire Flower
Moving right through the level
Landing on the flagpole
practice.explanation: Fireballs help but are optional and depend on a power-up, so they are secondary. Jumping and moving right are needed to finish a level, which makes them primary; landing on the flagpole is an outcome of jumping, not a separate mechanic.

practice.q: Pac-Man (1980) gives the player a joystick and no buttons. List its verbs, say what the main verb acts on, and explain why such a small verb set still supports skilled play.
practice.answer: Pac-Man has essentially one verb, steer (up, down, left, right through the maze). Steering acts on dots, power pellets, fruit and ghosts: passing over dots eats them, a power pellet turns the ghosts vulnerable, and steering away from or toward ghosts decides survival. Skill comes from routing: choosing paths that clear dots while keeping distance from ghosts, and timing power pellets to catch them.
practice.explanation: A good answer identifies steering as the single verb, names several objects that respond to it differently, and connects depth to the decisions about where to steer rather than to the number of verbs.

practice.q: Tetris has only three verbs. What best explains why it still rewards skill for years of play?
choices: The pieces are chosen to be easy to place
Each placement changes the board that every later decision must deal with
The game adds new verbs at higher levels
The score display makes players compare results
practice.explanation: Depth comes from consequences: every placement reshapes the board, so players plan several pieces ahead. The game never adds verbs, and the piece sequence is not arranged to help the player.

sections.title: Core, meta and session loops
reading: A verb becomes a loop when its result feeds the next decision. The **core loop** is the shortest cycle a player repeats: read the situation, act, see the result, read the new situation. In *Tetris* that cycle lasts as long as one piece, and Figure 2.1 traces it: a piece appears, the player picks a spot, slides and rotates, the piece locks, rows may clear, and the next piece appears. The researcher Emmanuel Guardiola argues that a list of a game’s actions misses this movement. His model of the **gameplay loop** describes play as the player passing again and again through states of activity inside the game system, which is closer to what designers actually shape [1].

Loops nest inside one another at different time scales. Studios commonly name three, though the terms come from practice rather than from a fixed standard, so expect other labels in other books. The core loop runs in seconds. The **session loop** is one sitting’s worth of play with a natural start and end: one game of *Tetris* from the first piece to topping out, one run in *Slay the Spire*, one evening’s attempt at *Super Mario Bros.* on a stock of lives. The **meta loop** runs across sessions. It covers whatever carries over from one sitting to the next and changes what the next session offers, such as new characters, a larger pool of cards or a harder difficulty setting. A useful test is to ask what the player keeps when they stop playing.

*Slay the Spire* shows all three clearly (Figure 2.2). The core loop is one turn of combat: you draw five cards, read the icons above each enemy that show what it intends to do next, spend your three energy on cards, and end your turn so the enemies act. Around it runs the session loop of a run. You pick a route up the map, enter a room (a fight, an event, a shop or a rest site) and take a reward, often a choice of one card from three, plus gold and sometimes a relic. Your deck changes, so the next fight plays differently. Outside that sits the meta loop. Your score from each run adds new cards and relics to the pool for later runs, and beating the third act with a character opens Ascension, 20 levels that each add a new handicap.

The point of nesting is that each outer loop changes the inputs of the loop inside it. A card picked in the session loop changes which hands you draw in the core loop; a card added to the pool in the meta loop changes which rewards appear in the session loop. Adams and Dormans describe this kind of structure as feedback: the output of one part of a system returns as input to another, and the shape of that return decides whether play accelerates, settles or spirals [2]. *Tetris* has a feedback loop of its own, drawn in purple in Figure 2.1. In a game started at level 0, every 10 lines raises the level and makes pieces fall faster, so success in the core loop makes the core loop harder. Chapter 3 studies loops like this in detail.

Not every game needs all three loops. The NES *Tetris* of 1989 has almost no meta loop: nothing you do in one game changes the rules of the next, and the only thing that carries over is a score to beat. People still compete at it decades later. The reverse rarely works. Players spend most of their time inside the core loop, so a meta loop of rewards and progress bars seldom rescues a core loop that is dull to repeat. That is why designers prototype the core loop first, often on paper, and play it many times before building anything around it. When you add an outer loop, ask what it gives the player: a reason to come back, a new decision, or only a number that goes up.

keyTerms.def: The shortest cycle of reading, acting and seeing results that a player repeats, usually lasting seconds.
The cycle that makes up one sitting of play with a natural start and end, such as a run, a match or a level.
The cycle that runs across sessions, through whatever carries over and changes later play.
Guardiola’s model of play as the player repeatedly passing through states of activity within the game system.
Loops at different time scales arranged so that each outer loop changes what the inner loop works with.

example.title: Worked example: finding the three loops of Super Mario Bros.
steps: Find the cycle measured in seconds. Mario meets an obstacle (a Goomba, a gap, a pipe), the player picks a speed and a moment to jump, Mario lands, and the next obstacle comes into view. That is the core loop.

Find one sitting’s worth of play. The player starts at World 1-1 with a stock of lives, clears levels by reaching the flagpole or the castle, loses a life when hit while small or when falling into a pit, and stops at game over or at the end. That is the session loop.
Ask what carries over when the console is switched off. The 1985 cartridge saves nothing, so the next session starts again from 1-1 with nothing new added to the game.

Look for the meta loop elsewhere. What carries over is the player’s own skill and knowledge: the timing of each jump, where enemies appear, where the hidden warp zones are. The meta loop lives in the player, not in the software.
example.takeaway: When a game stores nothing between sessions, the player’s growing skill becomes the meta loop.

misconception.myth: A strong meta loop, with daily rewards, levels and collectible extras, is what makes a game good.
misconception.fact: Meta loops give players reasons to return, but players spend most of their time in the core loop. NES *Tetris* has almost no meta loop and is still played competitively; a weak core loop wrapped in rewards tends to feel like a chore.

practice.q: In Slay the Spire, choosing one of three cards after a fight belongs mainly to which loop?
choices: The core loop
The meta loop
The session loop
None; it is a cosmetic choice
practice.explanation: Card rewards happen floor by floor within a single run, so they belong to the session loop. They change the core loop of later fights, and the cards available to be offered depend on the meta loop, but the choice itself is made inside the run.

practice.q: A chess player plays rated games at a club every week. Describe the core, session and meta loops of their chess, and say which loop the rating belongs to.
practice.answer: Core loop: one move cycle, in which the player reads the position, chooses and makes a move, and sees the opponent’s reply. Session loop: one game, from the opening to checkmate, resignation, a draw or a time loss. Meta loop: the season of club games, in which results change the player’s rating, which changes who they are paired against and how they prepare. The rating belongs to the meta loop, because it carries over between games and changes later sessions.
practice.explanation: A good answer gives the time scale of each loop, places the rating in the meta loop, and explains that it carries over and changes future play.

practice.q: A designer wants to change only the meta loop of their roguelike. Which change does that?
choices: Making the basic attack card deal 1 more damage
Adding an extra shop to every map
Letting a character’s cumulative score add new cards to the reward pool for future runs
Showing enemy intentions with clearer icons
practice.explanation: Only the cumulative score carries across runs. Card damage and intent icons act within the core loop, and an extra shop changes each run’s session loop.

sections.title: Game feel and juice
reading: Two games can share the same rules and still feel completely different in the hands. Steve Swink’s book *Game Feel* gave designers a vocabulary for that difference. He defines game feel as “real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space, with interactions emphasized by polish” [1]. Each part of the definition does work. **Real-time control** means the player steers continuously and the game answers fast enough that intention, action and response feel like one unbroken loop. **Simulated space** means there is a world with movement and collision for the controlled object to act in. **Polish** means the animation, effects and sound that sell an interaction without changing the simulation underneath [1]. The definition is deliberately narrow: by requiring real-time control, it leaves out turn-based games such as chess and *Slay the Spire*.

Swink breaks feel into parts a designer can adjust: input (the physical device), response (how the game turns input into motion), context (the spaces and obstacles that give motion meaning), polish, metaphor (what the object is meant to be) and rules [1]. On response, he draws on research about human perception to argue that the game must answer within roughly a tenth of a second for control to feel immediate [1]. Mario’s jump, which Swink analyzes in detail, is a model of response design. Hold the button longer and Mario jumps higher; build speed by running and the same jump carries farther. The player is not choosing among a few fixed jumps but shaping each one, which is how a single verb can carry a whole game.

Feel also comes from timing rules most players never see. In NES *Tetris*, holding left or right moves the piece one column at once, then waits 16 frames (about a quarter of a second at the console’s 60 frames per second) before repeating, and then moves one column every 6 frames, roughly 10 columns a second. This **delayed auto shift** stops a brief press from sending a piece too far, so slow play feels precise. But gravity rises with the level. At level 0 a piece falls one row every 48 frames; from level 19 it falls a row every 2 frames, and at level 29 a row every frame. At that speed a held direction cannot carry a piece across the well before it lands, so for decades players called level 29 the kill screen.

**Juice** is the informal name for polish turned up high: screen shake when something lands, particles when a block breaks, a sound and a flash for every hit. Researchers have tried to pin the idea down and test it. Kieran Hicks and colleagues asked game developers what makes feedback juicy and built a framework for analyzing it from their answers [2]. Experiments suggest juice helps, up to a point. Jesper Juul and Jason Begy built two versions of one game that played identically, one with minimal feedback and one with heavy, redundant sound and animation; players preferred the juicy version, but it did not make them play better [3]. Dominic Kao built four versions of an action role-playing game, with no, medium, high and extreme juiciness. Medium and high levels beat both none and extreme on player experience, motivation, play time and performance [4].

Two practical lessons follow. First, feel lives mostly in the core loop, because that is where the player’s hands spend their time, so tune response and context before anything else. Second, juice amplifies a loop that already works but cannot fix one that does not, and too much of it gets in the way, as Kao’s extreme condition showed [4]. A quick test is to switch the effects off: if the game is still worth playing, the polish is adding to it; if not, the problem lies deeper. Paper games have feel too. The slap of a card on the table in a speed game, the riffle of a shuffle and the click of chips are input and response in the physical world, and you can design your pocket card game around them.

keyTerms.def: Swink’s term for real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space, with interactions emphasized by polish.
How a game converts the player’s input into motion and other changes, including how quickly it does so.
The spaces, objects and obstacles that give a controlled motion its meaning.
Animation, effects and sound that emphasize an interaction without changing the simulation.
Heavy, often redundant audiovisual feedback added to make actions feel satisfying.
A rule that waits after the first move before a held direction starts repeating, as in NES Tetris.

example.title: Worked example: why level 29 stopped a generation of Tetris players
steps: Gravity: at level 29 a piece falls one row per frame. Falling about 18 rows to the floor of an empty well takes about 18 frames, or 18 ÷ 60.1 ≈ 0.30 seconds.
Shifting with a held button: the first column moves at once, the second after 16 frames, then one more every 6 frames. Moving 5 columns therefore takes 16 + 3 × 6 = 34 frames, or about 0.57 seconds.
Compare: the piece lands roughly a quarter of a second before it could reach the fifth column. Moves near the center still work, but the edges of the well are out of reach.

Check level 19 for contrast: 2 frames per row gives 36 frames to fall 18 rows, against 34 frames for the 5-column shift, a margin of 2 frames. The game is barely playable there with a held button, which matches the experience of players at that level.

Conclude: a timing rule chosen to make slow play feel precise set the practical ceiling of the whole game. (This simple model leaves out some details of the real code, such as the short pause before each new piece appears.)
example.takeaway: Feel and rules are not separate layers: a response rule tuned for comfort can decide what is possible at the highest skill.

misconception.myth: Game feel is about graphics, and adding more effects always makes a game feel better.
misconception.fact: Most of game feel comes from response and context: how quickly and how expressively the game answers input, and what the space asks of the player. Effects help only up to a point; in Kao’s study, extreme juiciness did worse than moderate amounts.

practice.q: A designer adds screen shake and a burst of particles whenever the player’s character lands, without changing the movement code. Which of Swink’s building blocks have they changed?
choices: Real-time control
Simulated space
Rules
Polish
practice.explanation: Screen shake and particles emphasize the landing without altering how the character moves or collides, which is exactly what Swink means by polish.

practice.q: Playtesters say a new platformer prototype feels stiff. The character reaches full speed the instant a direction is pressed, and every jump is the same height. Using this section, propose two changes and explain why each should help.
practice.answer: First, make jump height depend on how long the button is held, as in Super Mario Bros., so players shape each jump instead of choosing a fixed one. Second, give running a short acceleration so speed builds over time, and let speed change jump distance. Both changes make the response more expressive, so small differences in input produce visible differences in motion. Keep the response itself fast, within about a tenth of a second, so the extra nuance does not feel like lag.
practice.explanation: A strong answer names response as the problem, proposes variable jump height and some form of acceleration or momentum, and notes that expressiveness must not come at the cost of response time.

practice.q: In Kao’s study of four versions of an action RPG, which versions gave the best player experience?
choices: The version with no juiciness
The medium and high juiciness versions
The extreme juiciness version
All four were the same
practice.explanation: Medium and high juiciness beat both no juiciness and extreme juiciness, which suggests feedback helps up to a point and then gets in the way.

sections.title: Emergence
reading: **Emergence** is what happens when simple rules, interacting, produce patterns that no single rule describes; Salen and Zimmerman treat it as one of the defining properties of games as systems [5]. The cleanest demonstration is not a commercial game. In October 1970, Martin Gardner’s “Mathematical Games” column in *Scientific American* introduced a solitaire game invented by the mathematician John Conway, called Life [1]. The board is a grid of cells, each alive or dead. Each generation, a dead cell with exactly three live neighbors comes alive, a live cell with two or three live neighbors survives, and every other live cell dies [1]. That is the whole rulebook. Yet a five-cell shape called the **glider** crawls across the grid, rebuilding itself one cell over every four generations (Figure 2.3). No rule mentions movement.

Board games have shown emergence for centuries. The rules of chess fit on a page, yet in 1950 Claude Shannon estimated the number of possible chess games at around 10¹²⁰, far more than could ever be played [2]. From those rules came a body of knowledge the rules never mention: named openings, pawn structures, the advice that a knight on the edge of the board is weak. Players discovered all of it. Jesper Juul calls such games **games of emergence**, in which a few rules combine into large variation, and contrasts them with **games of progression**, in which the designer lays out a series of challenges with planned solutions, as in a classic adventure game [3]. Most games, he argues, mix the two [3].

Our running examples sit at different points on Juul’s scale. World 1-1 of *Super Mario Bros.* leans toward progression: the designers placed every Goomba and block, and Chapter 6 reads it as a planned lesson. *Tetris* leans toward emergence: seven shapes and a few rules produce a different board every game. *Slay the Spire* does both. Its acts and bosses form a progression, but its cards and relics combine in ways no one listed in advance. The card Corruption makes Skills cost nothing but exhausts each one as it is played; the relic Dead Branch adds a random card to your hand whenever a card is exhausted. Together they turn every free Skill into a fresh card, a combination players often name among the strongest in the game.

*The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild* (2017) built a whole open world on this idea. At the 2017 Game Developers Conference, director Hidemaro Fujibayashi, technical director Takuhiro Dohta and art director Satoru Takizawa described how the team began with a simple top-down prototype in the style of the original 1986 *Legend of Zelda*, in which tools combined, such as an arrow shot through a fire becoming a fire arrow [4]. The finished game rests on general rules about elements and the states of objects, which the team called a chemistry engine, so that effects multiply as rules meet [4]. You can see the result in ordinary play. Fire spreads through dry grass and its rising heat lifts a paraglider; a leaf’s gust can push a raft. The designers wrote rules, not solutions.

Emergence also happens between the rules and the players’ bodies. The delayed auto shift described in section 2.3 limits a held direction to about 10 columns a second, but every fresh press moves the piece at once. So players learned to press faster than the auto-shift. Thor Aackerlund is credited as the first to master this fast tapping, now called **hypertapping**. In 2020 a player known as Cheez popularized **rolling**, in which the fingers drum on the back of the controller and push it against a thumb resting on the direction pad, producing several presses per motion. With these techniques players passed level 29, and in December 2023 Gibson reached the crash at level 157. Emergence gives a game depth no one planned, but the same process yields exploits and dominant strategies, the subject of Chapter 3. Playtesting is the only reliable way to find either.

example.title: Worked example: stepping a glider forward by hand
steps: Write the glider as (row, column) cells: (1,2), (2,3), (3,1), (3,2), (3,3). Each cell has eight neighbors, including diagonals.
Check each live cell. (1,2) has one live neighbor, (2,3), so it dies. (3,1) has one, (3,2), so it dies. (2,3) has three, (3,2) has three and (3,3) has two, so all three survive.

Check dead cells next to the pattern for exactly three live neighbors. (2,1) touches (1,2), (3,1) and (3,2): it is born. (4,2) touches (3,1), (3,2) and (3,3): it is born. No other dead cell has exactly three.

Generation 1 is (2,1), (2,3), (3,2), (3,3), (4,2): still five cells, in a new shape. Repeating the same three checks three more times gives (2,3), (3,4), (4,2), (4,3), (4,4), which is the starting shape moved one row down and one column right.
example.takeaway: Motion appears at the level of the pattern, even though every rule talks only about single cells and their neighbors.

misconception.myth: Emergent gameplay just means random gameplay.
misconception.fact: Life and chess contain no randomness at all, yet both are classic examples of emergence. Emergence comes from rules interacting with each other and with players’ choices; randomness, like the piece order in Tetris, adds variety but does not create emergence by itself.

practice.q: In Conway’s Life, a dead cell has exactly two live neighbors. What happens to it in the next generation?
choices: It comes alive
It stays dead
It comes alive only if it was alive before
It dies again
practice.explanation: Birth needs exactly three live neighbors. The two-or-three rule applies only to cells that are already alive, so a dead cell with two neighbors stays dead.

practice.q: Using Juul’s distinction, compare a crossword puzzle with poker. Which is closer to a game of emergence, and why?
practice.answer: A crossword is a game of progression: the setter designed one intended solution, and once solved it offers little new play. Poker is closer to a game of emergence: a small set of rules about betting and hand rankings combines with players’ choices to produce endless variation, including bluffing and reading opponents, which the rules never mention.
practice.explanation: A good answer ties progression to a designed sequence with planned solutions and emergence to variation arising from rules interacting with player choices, and gives at least one emergent behavior in poker.

practice.q: A designer wants a fantasy game to support player solutions nobody scripted. Which rule is most systemic?
choices: The door to the third dungeon opens when the player uses the Ruby Key
Any flammable object catches fire when touched by any flame, and burning objects light flammable things next to them
The boss is weak to the Silver Sword
The quest giver’s dialogue changes after the second quest
practice.explanation: A general rule about all flammable objects and all flames can combine with many other objects in unplanned ways. The other options are special cases that each work in one scripted situation.

interactives.title: One turn of the Tetris core loop
interactives.intro: Put the steps of a single piece’s life in order, then check against Figure 2.1. Notice which steps belong to the player and which to the game.
steps: A new piece appears at the top of the well, and the next piece shows in the preview
The player reads the board and picks a landing spot
The player slides and rotates the piece while gravity pulls it down
The piece touches the stack and locks in place
Any completed rows clear, and the score and line count go up
The game checks the line total and, at every 10 lines, raises the level so pieces fall faster
interactives.explain: Only steps 2 and 3 belong to the player; the rest are the game’s response. The last step is the feedback that ties the core loop to the session loop: playing well speeds the loop up.

interactives.title: Sort the loops by time scale
interactives.intro: Decide whether each activity belongs to the core loop (seconds), the session loop (one sitting) or the meta loop (across sessions). Ask what the player keeps after they stop.

items.text: Tetris: sliding and rotating a falling piece into place
items.why: One piece takes seconds and is the shortest repeated cycle.

items.text: Slay the Spire: spending three energy on cards, then ending the turn
items.why: One turn of combat is the game’s core loop.

items.text: Super Mario Bros.: running up to a Goomba and jumping on it
items.why: A few seconds of read, act and land.

items.text: Tetris: one game from level 0 until the stack tops out
items.why: A single game is one sitting with a clear start and end.

items.text: Slay the Spire: one run from the first floor to a win or a death
items.why: The run is the session loop; the deck you build vanishes when it ends.

items.text: Super Mario Bros.: playing from World 1-1 onward on one stock of lives
items.why: The 1985 game saves nothing, so all of this progress lives inside one sitting.

items.text: Slay the Spire: opening the next Ascension level after a win
items.why: It carries over between runs and changes the rules of later runs.

items.text: Slay the Spire: new cards joining the reward pool as a character’s total score grows
items.why: Score accumulates across runs and changes what later runs can offer.

interactives.title: Gravity versus the held button in NES Tetris
interactives.intro: Set gravity to 48 frames per row (level 0), then 2 (levels 19 to 28), then 1 (level 29). Keep the shift at 5 columns and watch the spare time. Then try shorter shifts at gravity 1.

outputs.label: Time to shift by holding the button
Spare time (negative means the piece lands first)

interactives.takeaway: The held-button shift takes the same 0.57 seconds for 5 columns at every level, while fall time shrinks with gravity. At 2 frames per row the margin is about 0.03 seconds; at 1 frame per row it is negative, which is why level 29 was called the kill screen until players learned to tap faster than the auto-shift. The model uses the NES rules (first column at once, the next after 16 frames, then every 6 frames) and ignores the brief pause before each piece appears.

interactives.title: The kill screen that was not
interactives.intro: NES Tetris (1989) set a held direction to repeat after 16 frames and then every 6 frames, and made pieces fall one row per frame from level 29. For many years, level 29 was treated as the end of the game. Think through each question before revealing the answer.

steps.a: No. Nothing in the code ends the game there and nothing glitches. It was an emergent limit: the interaction of the gravity table and the delayed auto shift made it practically impossible to reach the edges of the well by holding a direction, so players gave it the name kill screen.

steps.q: What rule did players find to work around it?
steps.a: Every fresh press moves the piece immediately, without the 16-frame wait. Tapping faster than the auto-shift repeats beats the held button. Thor Aackerlund pioneered this hypertapping; in 2020 rolling, popularized by a player known as Cheez, produced even faster presses by drumming the fingers on the back of the controller.

steps.q: Where did the game actually end?
steps.a: With rolling, players kept going far beyond level 29, and on 21 December 2023 Willis Gibson, aged 13, reached level 157, where the game crashed. The real limit turned out to be a fault in the code, not anything the designers planned.

steps.q: What should a designer take from this?
steps.a: Emergence can come from rules meeting human hands as well as rules meeting rules, and no one can predict it fully by reading the rules. Here it gave a 1989 game a competitive life lasting decades. The only way to discover such behavior, good or bad, is to watch real people play.

slides.title: Chapter 2: Core loops and mechanics
bullets: Verbs and core mechanics: what the player does
Core, session and meta loops
Game feel and juice
Emergence: simple rules, complex play
slides.notes: Chapter 1 gave us mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics. Today we look closely at the mechanics the player touches, and at how they repeat, feel and combine. By the end you will define the core loop of your pocket card game.

slides.title: Verbs: the player’s side of the rules
bullets: Tetris: move, rotate, drop
Super Mario Bros.: walk, run, jump
Slay the Spire: play a card, end turn, choose a path, choose a reward
Test: do your verbs fit on a sticky note?
slides.notes: The rules are the designer’s view; verbs are what the player experiences. Start every analysis by translating inputs into verbs.

slides.title: Core mechanics
bullets: Salen and Zimmerman: the essential play activity players perform again and again
Sicart: methods invoked by agents for interacting with the game world
Primary mechanics beat challenges; secondary ones help
Good verbs act on many objects
slides.notes: Mario’s jump stomps enemies, bumps blocks, clears pipes and reaches the flagpole. That economy, one verb meeting many objects, is what people mean by a strong core mechanic.

slides.title: The Tetris core loop
bullets: Piece appears, player reads the board
Slide and rotate while gravity pulls
Lock, clear rows, score
Every 10 lines: faster pieces
slides.notes: Use Figure 2.1. Only two steps belong to the player. The purple feedback arrow makes success speed the loop up, which Chapter 3 studies as a feedback loop.

slides.title: Loops at three time scales
bullets: Core loop: seconds
Session loop: one sitting, such as a run or a game
Meta loop: across sessions
Test: what does the player keep when they stop?
slides.notes: These labels come from studio practice and vary between teams. The idea that matters is nesting: each outer loop changes the inner one.

slides.title: Nested loops in Slay the Spire
bullets: Core: draw 5, read intents, spend 3 energy, end turn
Session: map, room, reward, deck changes
Meta: score adds cards and relics; wins open Ascension
A meta loop rarely rescues a dull core loop
slides.notes: Walk through Figure 2.2 from the inside out. Then compare NES Tetris, which has almost no meta loop and is still played competitively.

slides.title: Game feel
bullets: Swink: real-time control, simulated space, polish
Input, response, context, polish, metaphor, rules
Response within about a tenth of a second
Mario’s jump: hold longer, jump higher
slides.notes: Feel is mostly response and context. The NES Tetris delayed auto shift shows how one timing rule can make slow play precise and fast play impossible.

slides.title: Juice: what the evidence says
bullets: Juice: heavy audiovisual feedback
Juul and Begy: preferred, but no better play
Kao: medium and high beat none and extreme
Juice amplifies a good loop; it cannot fix a bad one
slides.notes: Treat juice like seasoning. Switch the effects off: if the game is still worth playing, the polish is helping.

slides.title: Emergence
bullets: Conway’s Life: three rules, a gliding pattern
Chess: about 10^120 possible games (Shannon)
Juul: games of emergence versus games of progression
Slay the Spire: Corruption plus Dead Branch
slides.notes: Use Figure 2.3. No rule of Life mentions motion, yet the glider moves. Ask students to find the emergent strategy in a game they play.

slides.title: Designing for emergence
bullets: Breath of the Wild: general rules about elements and object states
Write rules, not solutions
Players add emergence too: hypertapping and rolling
Only playtesting reveals it
slides.notes: The Tetris case shows emergence between rules and hands. It gave the game decades of life, and the same process produces the exploits we will hunt in Chapters 3 and 4.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Verbs and core mechanics are the player’s view of the rules
Loops nest: core, session, meta
Feel comes from response, context and polish
Simple rules can combine into play nobody wrote
slides.notes: Before the quiz, write the verbs and core loop of one game you play. Then do the same for your pocket card game in the challenge.

quiz.q: Which statement best matches Salen and Zimmerman’s definition of a core mechanic?
choices: The game’s setting and theme
The essential play activity players perform again and again
The rule that decides who wins
The most complex rule in the game
quiz.explanation: A core mechanic is the repeated activity at the heart of play. Theme, victory conditions and complexity are separate matters.

quiz.q: A new puzzle game has one verb, swap two adjacent tiles. Playtesters find it shallow. Which change most directly deepens the core mechanic without adding verbs?
choices: Adding a soundtrack
Adding a second, unrelated minigame
Adding a level map with stars to collect
Making tile types respond differently to a swap, so one swap can trigger different effects
quiz.explanation: A verb gains depth when more objects respond to it in different ways, as Mario’s jump does. Music, an extra minigame and a progress map add nothing to the swap itself.

quiz.q: In Slay the Spire, which of these belongs to the meta loop?
choices: Ascension levels opened by winning runs
Drawing five cards each turn
Choosing a path on the map
Buying a card at a shop
quiz.explanation: Ascension carries over between runs. Drawing cards is part of the core loop; paths and shops belong to the session loop of a run.

quiz.q: A mobile game has a tedious core loop but generous daily rewards and a long progression track. Based on this chapter, what is the most likely result?
choices: Players will enjoy it because the meta loop is strong
The rewards will make the core loop feel exciting
Players may return for rewards but find most of their time a chore
The session loop will disappear
quiz.explanation: Players spend most of their time in the core loop. A meta loop can supply reasons to return but rarely makes a dull core loop enjoyable.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of Swink’s definition of game feel?
choices: Turn-based strategic choice
A branching story
Real-time control of virtual objects
High-resolution graphics
quiz.explanation: Swink defines game feel as real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space, with interactions emphasized by polish.

quiz.q: In NES Tetris, gravity at some level is 3 frames per row. A piece must fall 18 rows and you need to hold the button to shift it 5 columns (34 frames). About how much time do you have to spare?
choices: About 0.33 seconds
About 0.03 seconds
None; the piece lands first
About 1.5 seconds
quiz.explanation: Falling takes 18 × 3 = 54 frames, and the shift takes 34, leaving 20 frames, or 20 ÷ 60.1 ≈ 0.33 seconds.

quiz.q: Why is the glider in Conway’s Life a good example of emergence?
choices: It was programmed to move diagonally
Its motion arises from rules that only describe single cells and their neighbors
It appears randomly
Conway designed it as the game’s goal
quiz.explanation: No rule mentions movement. The glider’s travel is a pattern-level result of birth, survival and death rules applied to every cell.

quiz.q: A designer replaces 30 scripted puzzle solutions with three general rules: fire burns wood, wind pushes light objects, and metal conducts electricity. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: Players will find fewer ways to solve puzzles
Every puzzle will have exactly one solution
The game becomes a pure game of progression
Players will find solutions the designer did not plan, including some that break puzzles
quiz.explanation: General rules interact, which is the systemic approach of Breath of the Wild. That produces unplanned solutions, good and bad, so the designer needs playtests to find them.

challenge.title: Diagram three core loops
challenge.prompt: Choose three games from different genres; one may be a running example from this book. For each, list its verbs, draw its core loop as a cycle of four to six steps, and mark which steps belong to the player and which to the game. Then name the session loop and the meta loop (or explain why the game has none) and identify one way an outer loop changes the core loop.
challenge.deliverable: For each game: a verb list, a core loop written as numbered steps that return to the start (or a described diagram), a one-sentence session loop, a one-sentence meta loop, and one sentence on how an outer loop changes the core loop.
rubric: Lists verbs as player actions rather than buttons or themes
Each core loop is a closed cycle in which the result of one step feeds the next
Distinguishes player steps from game responses
Places session and meta loops at the right time scales and explains how one changes the core loop

challenge.title: Pocket card game: define the core loop
challenge.prompt: Return to the pocket card game you started in Chapter 1. Write its verbs as moves between zones (deck, hand, table, discard pile, opponent). Then write the core loop of one turn as four to six steps, the session loop that makes up one game, and either a meta loop or a reason it has none. Play three turns alone with real cards, note where the loop stalls or a verb goes unused, and make one rule change in response.
challenge.deliverable: A verb list, the core loop as numbered steps, one paragraph on the session loop and meta loop, and a short playtest note (three turns) ending with the one rule change you made and why.
rubric: Verbs are concrete, card-moving actions that a new player could perform from the description
The core loop closes: the end of a turn sets up the next decision
The session loop has a clear start and end condition
The playtest note reports an observed problem and a specific rule change that addresses it

readings.citation: Swink, S. (2009). Game feel: A game designer’s guide to virtual sensation. Morgan Kaufmann.
readings.why: The standard book on game feel. Read the opening chapters for the definition and building blocks, and the analysis of Super Mario Bros. for response design in practice.

readings.citation: Salen, K., & Zimmerman, E. (2003). Rules of play: Game design fundamentals. MIT Press.
readings.why: Read its discussion of the core mechanic and its chapter on games as emergent systems for the definitions used in sections 2.1 and 2.4.

readings.citation: Adams, E., & Dormans, J. (2012). Game mechanics: Advanced game design. New Riders.
readings.why: Shows how to treat mechanics as interacting systems and feedback structures; it sets up Chapters 3 and 4.

readings.citation: Juul, J. (2002). The open and the closed: Games of emergence and games of progression. In F. Mäyrä (Ed.), Computer games and digital cultures: Conference proceedings (pp. 323–329). Tampere University Press.
readings.why: A short, clear paper on games of emergence and games of progression. Supports section 2.4.

readings.citation: Sicart, M. (2008). Defining game mechanics. Game Studies, 8(2).
readings.why: A careful definition of game mechanics and of core, primary and secondary mechanics. Free to read online in the journal Game Studies.
